newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU urged to take soft approach to Internet laws.
newsitem.headline: EU urged to take soft approach to Internet laws.

text.p: Business leaders and politicians from all over the world Monday urged the European Union (EU) to take a soft line toward cyberspace laws.

In meetings of more than 40 government ministers and some 80 business leaders at the EU's Global Information Network conference, participants across the board called for more private-sector efforts to establish fair play on the Internet.
The conference is preparing a non-binding statement to guide European policy on issues ranging from data security and privacy to pornography and extremist writings on the Internet.

The United States, while only an observer at the event, stole some of the conference's thunder last week when President Clinton presented a framework on electronic commerce calling for a "free-trade zone" in cyberspace.

U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley, carrying Clinton's framework to Europe, said governments should let the marketplace decide on Internet standards and controls and invited European support for Clinton's initiative.

"We have one option -- to move forward as partners," Daley said. "To do less is to risk turning this next great economic stage into another dividing line among nations, where language, culture, geography, currency, history and technology still keep us from working together."
Daley emphasised to reporters a free-trade zone only means no new barriers would be erected. Existing taxes would stay.
"We do believe there should be no new taxes that discriminate against the Internet," he said. "Existing taxes, I would assume, would continue, as would sales tax."
Consumer commerce via the Internet is expected to surge to $50 billion per year by 2000 from around $2 billion now.
But EU officials were unsure EU ministers would commit to not imposing new tariffs or taxes on Internet commerce.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt also called for as little regulation as possible and urged all governments, including the United States, to deregulate encryption software used to protect data from being read by others on the Internet.

"Users can only protect themselves against having data manipulated, destroyed or spied on through the use of strong encryption procedures," Rexrodt said in the text of his opening statements. "That is why we have to use all of our powers to promote such procedures instead of blocking them."

Business leaders also urged governments to take a "light hand" in Internet regulation, with several charging EU countries such as Germany and France with adopting rules prohibiting investment and putting European companies at a disadvantage.

"The multimedia industry is marked by large alliances. And it is important to note that American companies are leading such alliances while in Europe it is the exception," said Thomas Middelhoff, designated chairman of Bertelsmann AG , Europe's biggest media conglomerate.
Middelhoff said German data security rules, French encryption laws and confusing jurisdiction between Germany's federal and state governments were European companies' main hurdles.
Instead of government, George Vradenburg, senior vice president of America Online Inc., said the market would drive companies to provide appropriate safety and security.
"Our consumer customers want us to give them protection against child pornography," he said. "Businesses are demanding that we make electronic commerce secure."
Canadian Industry Minister John Manley told reporters no government could control the rapid development of cyberspace.
"The public sector is unable to contemplate wisely the regulative or legislative rules that need to be in place when development is as rapid as it is," he said.
